1000069.etyen:
Internationalism, based on French Luxembourg and German Luxemburg. Both forms ultimately continue Middle High German Luccelemburc, from Old High German Lucilinburhuc, first recorded in a Latin deed from 963 and traditionally interpreted as “little castle”, from luzil (“little”) and burg (“castle, fortress”).
The name originally referred to the castle and the settlement that developed around it, and was later extended to the surrounding territory. The modern country, its capital, the Belgian province and the canton ultimately derive their names from this place-name.

1001605.etyen:
From the older Danish–Norwegian digraph ⟨Aa⟩, used to represent the long vowel which developed from Old Norse á /ɑː/. The doubling of ⟨a⟩ originally indicated vowel length. In mainland Scandinavian, the vowel became rounded to /ɔː/ and was later raised to /oː/ in many varieties.
The Swedish letter ⟨Å⟩ developed graphically by writing the second ⟨a⟩ above the first, where it was eventually reduced to a ring. Norwegian retained ⟨Aa⟩ for several centuries under Danish orthographic influence. ⟨Å⟩ was permitted in Riksmål in 1907 and officially replaced ⟨Aa⟩ in ordinary Norwegian spelling through t
